sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source straddles the area between the Campania and Basilicata regions, just south of the Vulture volcano, and belongs to the oblique to right-lateral strike-slip system that affects the central and southern Adriatic foreland. This Source is a near-vertical, ca. N-dipping, fault to the east of the main extensional axis of the southern Apennines.
Historical and instrumental catalogues (Boschi et al., 2000; Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006; Guidoboni et al., 2007) show a sparse intermediate seismicity in this region but it was hit by two of the strongest earthquakes of Italyâ€™s seismic history. These were the 8 September 1694 (Mw 6.9) and the well known 23 November 1980 (Mw 6.9) Irpinia-Basilicata earthquakes. The area was also affected by the 7 June 1910 (Mw 5.9, Irpinia-Basilicata) event.
This Source is thought to be a part of the oblique right-lateral, strike-slip fault system that would affect the entire seismogenic domain east of the southern Apennines backbone, and possibly of the central ones too. The region is clearly characterized by the occurrence of two major catastrophic earthquakes in a remarkably small area, i.e. their respective epicenters, both located with good confidence (the 1694 event has an abundant and strong intensity pattern that well constrains the epicentral zone; the 1980 event has precise instrumental location) lie 5-6 km from one another. Keeping in mind that (1) the fault length (size, in fact) that is needed to release the major seismic moment associated to either earthquake well exceeds 25 km (seismic moment, of course, is precisely documented for the 1980 event, while it can be obtained from Mw in the case of the 1694 one), and that (2) field data by Pantosti and Valensise (1990) and paleoseismological data by Pantosti et al. (1993) have demonstrated that the 1694 earthquake was not caused by the fault responsible for the 1980 one, one has to conclude that a further, major seismogenic fault lies just a few km east of the large fault system known along the main extensional axis of the southern Apennines. Considering the possible scenarios of interaction between major, closely located faults (i.e. ruling out solutions that would be geologically unfeasible), this line of reasoning opens the hypothesis concerning the possible geometry and kinematics of the causative fault for the 1694 event. We believe that such fault lies just east of the easternmost fault that caused a sub-event of the 1980 sequence, possibly slightly deeper than this structure and at an angle with it, showing a right-lateral component in the sense of motion.
The strike of this Source was based on that of the mapped regional structures. The dip was based on geological data and geometrical considerations. The rake represents oblique right-lateral strike slip, inferred from seismological data. The minimum and maximum depth were based on geological and subsurface data. The slip rate was inferred from geodynamic considerations for the tectonic environment that includes this Source.
